title: VPC orchestration: elevator scripts, objection maps, and competitive framing
summary: Working playbook for sales + SEs: short elevator scripts tailored to CISO/CloudSec/Platform buyers, a mapped objection-response tree specific to private/VPC deployments, and crisp competitive angles versus managed cloud endpoints and self-hosted runtimes.
body:
Purpose and audience:
This is a condensed, field-usable playbook for Account Execs and Solutions Engineers handling regulated buyers (finance, healthcare, gov). The goal: get to a technical yes quickly by aligning control-plane language to buyer risk models, surface low-friction POC paths, and neutralize the common procurement and security objections we see in early-stage conversations.

Structure:
- 30s elevator for each persona
- Objection map (decision tree) with collateral link suggestions
- Differentiation bullets vs (1) hyperscaler managed endpoints, (2) vendor-hosted APIs, (3) self-hosted open-source stacks
- Rapid POC and procurement playbook

Persona elevator scripts (short, testable):
- CISO (risk-focused): "Redwood lets you run LLM inference behind your VPC with only a thin control-plane agent in our SaaS console. All customer data and KV caches stay on your network; the control plane transmits only non-sensitive telemetry we agree on and can be encrypted with your KMS. That gives you fast time-to-value without shipping sensitive logs to third parties."
- Cloud Security Architect (network/ops-focused): "We support an agented deployment model: orchestration via a customer-controlled control plane endpoint in your VPC, optional on-prem orchestration for air-gapped sites, and an operator role that never sees plaintext models or data. We'll provide Terraform modules and a hardened bootstrap artifact for audits."
- ML Platform Lead (engineering/ops): "Same runtime, same API, different hosting: you get Redwood’s batching, KV-cache, and quantized runtime optimizations deployed into your cluster. We keep API compatibility so your integration work is identical whether you start hosted or go private."

Common buyer objections and mapped responses (decision-tree style):
- Objection: "We can't allow any external control plane touching our tenant metadata or logs."
  Response options: 
  1) Offer a "control-plane telemetry contract": a scoped, auditable list of telemetry keys + a signed attestation showing only lifecycle events and no payloads are transmitted. Provide an example NDAs and telemetry schema.
  2) If they require zero egress, propose agent-only mode + local control plane: Redwood provides the orchestrator as a deployable container image and a small management UI that runs inside their VPC.
  Collateral: telemetry schema doc, local-control-plane whitepaper, compliance checklist.

- Objection: "What about proofs for compliance teams (SOC2 / ISO / FedRAMP)?"
  Response: 
  1) Present our compliance readiness pack: SOC2-type control mappings for private deployments, KMS/HSM integration runbook, and sample audit logs showing redaction and retention policies.
  2) Offer a scoped SOC2 readiness workshop or an on-site / virtual architecture review with our security engineering team.
  Collateral: SOC2-readiness-summary.pdf, runbook for KMS handoff, sample redacted logs.

- Objection: "How do we prove data never leaves region / we don't expose secrets?"
  Response: 
  - Technical: show network flow diagrams (agent-only path, egress blocker rules, service mesh examples), provide a reproducible test harness that generates synthetic requests and uses packet captures to validate.
  - Contractual: include an egress guarantee clause and SLO for local-only inference in the contract.
  Collateral: network-diagrams, egress-guarantee-term-template.docx, packet-capture-testcase.zip

- Objection: "This sounds like a heavy operational lift compared to calling an API."
  Response: 
  - Show the staged onboarding: sandbox agent (30–60 min), basic inference POC (1–3 days), production rollout with autoscaling and cost-tuning (2–4 weeks). Provide a managed onboarding offer: Redwood engineers run the first POC and hand off runbooks.
  Collateral: 30-60-90 day POC timeline slide, onboarding SOW template.

Competitive framing (concise bullets that SEs can use in conversation):
- Versus hyperscaler model endpoints: 
  - Hyperscalers tie you to region/instance types and opaque runtime optimizations. Redwood offers parity of SLOs but with a control-plane contract and optional agent-only mode so you can keep operational ownership.
  - Talk track: cost predictability + no vendor lock-in for model variants.
- Versus API-first LLM vendors (hosted APIs): 
  - Hosted vendors often lack the deep runtime optimizations (KV cache reuse, attention kernels) at customer scale; moving on-prem to match their performance means heavy lift. Redwood provides the same serving runtime you get hosted, inside your network.
- Versus DIY/self-hosted open-source stack: 
  - DIY requires building autoscaling, continuous-batching, quantization ops, and rollout controls. Redwood packages those into the runtime and provides upgrade/rollback tooling and eval-based regression alerts. Also offer short-term access to Redwood engineers for the handoff.

Collateral and artifacts to have ready (lowest-friction first):
- Short: 1-pager: "What the private agent sends (telemetry schema)"
- Short: "Agent-only deployment checklist (network ports, KMS, bootstrap)"
- Medium: runbook for KMS/HSM integration and key-handshake sequence
- Medium: POC timeline + SOW template for security review
- Long: local-control-plane architecture whitepaper + FIPS-capable build notes

POC playbook (practical recommended path):
1) Pre-POC: NDA + telemetry schema + proposed egress contract draft
2) Day 0: grant sandbox tenant, deploy agent in their dev VPC using our terraform module, verify connectivity
3) Day 1–3: run canonical prompt set, validate redaction/retention config, capture network traces
4) Week 1–2: performance tuning (batch sizes, KV cache warmup), map cost/perf tradeoffs, provide simple cost model
5) Week 3–4: production run and rollout plan (canary %s, fallback to hosted variants)

Sales aids (quick copy):
- CISO email opener: "We’ve been working with several regulated customers on an agent-only option that keeps all inference data in your VPC and only exchanges a pre-agreed, minimal telemetry set. Can we walk your security team through the telemetry contract and KMS handoff this week?"
- Procurement reply: "We can include a region-bound egress guarantee and an explicit telemetry attestation in the master agreement. Example term and a one-page summary attached."

Open questions / things to finalize:
- Exact telemetry keys that are considered "diagnostic-only" vs "sensitive" (need legal + privacy to sign off).
- Pricing model for fully agented/on-prem control plane (monthly infra + optional managed service hours vs fixed-seat license).
- Formalized template for egress guarantee in Master Services Agreement.

Notes to SEs (tactical):
- Always surface the agent-only mode early for highly regulated buyers — it immediately reframes the conversation from "trusted vendor" to "vendor tooling inside your trust boundary." 
- Bring a network diagram to the first architecture call — buyers respond well to concrete visuals.
- Use the telemetry schema as a conversation artifact (not just a PDF). Walk through each key and why it exists.

Draft collateral checklist (who to ask for what):
- Security eng: sample audit logs + telemetry schema (Priya)
- Product infra: terraform modules + agent bootstrap artifacts (Liam)
- Legal: draft egress clause and telemetry attestation template (Ethan)

Unresolved items for product: 
- Ship a certified "local-control-plane" bootstrap image and a minimal management UI for customers that cannot accept any external control plane. Estimate: 8–10 week eng effort.
- Define supported KMS providers and HSM flow and document FIPS scope.

Tone and rhetorical guidelines for SEs: 
- Be specific and concrete — regulated buyers want artifacts, not promises.
- Use contractual language when buyers ask for guarantees (egress guarantee, telemetry attestation).
- Differentiate technically (runtime parity + ops tools) and contractually (egress, telemetry, audit artifacts).

Bottom line (one-liner for decks): "Redwood private runs your inference under your roof: same high-performance runtime, auditable control-plane behavior, and contract-backed egress and telemetry guarantees that let regulated teams move faster with less risk."
